query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored phase‐selective recrystallization annealing treatment will simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys by selectively recrystallizing the soft phase while preserving a skeletal hard phase network.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a duplex microstructure composed of softer (ductile) and harder (strength-providing) phases in its as-cast or conventionally processed state.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal annealing protocol designed to induce selective recrystallization of the soft phase without altering the hard phase network.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be conducted at an annealing temperature and duration chosen to recrystallize only the soft phase (e.g., in the approximate temperature range reported for phase-selective recrystallization) under quasi-static room temperature mechanical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure comprising a fully recrystallized, soft matrix embedded within an unaltered, hard-phase skeleton.
generation.mechanism: By recrystallizing only the soft phase, the alloy develops a microstructure with enhanced strain hardening (due to the soft, deformable phase) and retained strength (from the unchanged hard phase). This duality tailors the strain partitioning during deformation, overcoming the conventional trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (untreated eutectic HEA), the phase-selectively recrystallized alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with increased uniform elongation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or conventionally annealed condition without selective phase recrystallization.
generation.boundary: This improvement is likely limited to eutectic alloys possessing clearly distinct soft and hard phases and could be sensitive to the exact annealing parameters; overly aggressive treatments may lead to complete recrystallization or coarsening that negate the intended benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal annealing conditions (temperature, time) and the magnitude of strength and ductility improvements may vary with alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic HEA samples. Subject one set to the proposed phase-selective recrystallization treatment while leaving the second set untreated as a control. Conduct standardized tensile testing (measuring yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility) and perform detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/TEM) to verify the presence of a selectively recrystallized soft phase with an intact hard phase network.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility relative to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the selective recrystallization of the soft phase with an intact hard phase network, then the intervention does not support the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text:
Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile

Abstract: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa.
